item.title: Dana White confused after UFC reporter's long-winded question: 'What the f— did you just ask me?'
item.description: Dana White's stunned reaction to a rambling question stole the UFC 334 post-fight presser as Ciryl Gane and Kayla Harrison defended their titles.
item.content:encoded:
UFC 334 was a massive event that saw Ciryl Gane survive Josh Hokit, Kayla Harrison defeating the legendary Amanda Nunes and Stephen Thompson ending his career on the highest of notes.

It appeared UFC president Dana White was left more flabbergasted by a long-winded question he received in the post-fight press conference than he did by anything he saw in the cage at Madison Square Garden on Saturday night.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The reporter prefaced his question about White "cooking up" MSG cards and it was a long journey to get White to respond to what he was actually asking – about whether White thinks about the battles he had to go through to get to this point in UFC.

"What the f--- did you just ask me?" White responded in apparent shock. "What did you just ask me? ‘You think about the battles throughout the time like times like today? Do you think about the war?’ Are you saying all the hard work and you know all the battles?"

The reporter asked whether he thinks about it at all or just when he asks him.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Just when you ask me," White retorted.

White had a smile on his face the entire time and the exchange was less than contentious.

But the UFC executive had plenty to smile about.

Gane and Hokit went through a five-round war, which ended with Gane winning via unanimous decision to retain the UFC Heavyweight Championship. Harrison defended the UFC Women’s Bantamweight Championship when she got Nunes to tap out.

Thompson, known as "Wonderboy" nailed Charles Radtke with a spinning-wheel kick in the third round during their preliminary bout. The TKO put an end on his career and was considered the "Performance of the Night."

item.title: Lions star’s knee buckles celebrating sack of Patriots’ Drake Maye as both injured on same play
item.description: Aidan Hutchinson injured his right knee during a sack celebration at Munich's Allianz Arena on the same play that Drake Maye hurt his ankle.
item.content:encoded:
The first quarter of the NFL game in Munich's Allianz Arena has been an injury disaster.

Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson injured his right knee and New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye suffered an ankle injury. Both are out of the game.

Both were apparently injured on the same play when Hutchinson sacked Maye.

DRAKE MAYE TELLS REPORTERS THEY DON'T KNOW 'WHAT THEY'RE TALKING ABOUT' DURING GERMANY PRESS CONFERENCE

Maye left the field, limping slowly back to the Patriots' locker room, and is questionable to return. He was replaced in the lineup by Tommy DeVito.

Hutchinson injured himself in the most unorthodox and unfortunate manner after his sack of Maye – during his sack celebration.

The former Michgan standout sacked Maye on a key third down passing situation. He arose and immediately separated to celebrate.

That celebration involved Hutchinson leaping into the air with his clenched right hand raised in celebration.

And when Hutchinson hit the ground, his right knee buckled and the Lions defensive end crumpled to the field at Munich's Allianz Arena.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Hutchinson was clutching his right knee as he lay on the field.

He was eventually taken into the Lions' medical tent and then walked into the team's locker room.

The Lions said Hutchinson is questionable to return to the game.

Hutchinson has five sacks this season. He missed all but five games in 2024 when he suffered a broken tibia and fibula on his left leg.

item.title: Golf influencer Claire Hogle from the bunker, Caroline Wozniacki's ladies night & McConaughey-Manning beat LSU
item.description: Paige Spiranac calls Claire Hogle a "beautiful golf fairy" after her bunker content, while Bigfoot sighting emails flood the inbox from readers.
item.content:encoded:
A few years ago, headlines like "Claire Hogle Could Be The Next Paige Spiranac" were being written about the now 27-year-old golf influencer. It turns out Paige Spiranac is the next Paige Spiranac. She's still dominating the golf influencer game.

But that headline and those like it were an acknowledgment of the type of golf content the former Cal State San Marcos golfer brought to the table. More than four years after giving the golf influencer world a jolt, Claire is still at it.

She still calls herself a "huge golf gal" and she's still following the playbook written by the top golf influencer on the planet. This bunker never stood a chance.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This is my kind of golf. It's not about where the ball ends up, it's about the journey. Some journeys involve swinging your way out of the sand and turning it into content.

It's working for Claire. She shows up, she puts in the work, and she's earned the respect of her fellow influencers. That includes the very top.

Paige had this to say about her work from the bunker, "The most beautiful golf fairy!"

CLICK HERE FOR COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

I had the multiview going for most of the day yesterday, but I was multitasking for much of it. Yesterday was a big day in the Joseph household. It was the day every year I get to drag out all of my wife's Christmas decorations.

Thankfully, we're extending this madness into another weekend because she decided we needed new trees. So while most of the decorations are up, not the outdoor ones quite yet, we still have the joy of putting up two trees to look forward to.

Anyway, I did see Matthew McConaughey and Arch Manning lead Texas to victory in Death Valley and hand Lane Kiffin and company loss number four, which isn't going to cut it in the SEC.

I caught some of Michigan getting steamrolled by No. 16 Oregon, which you really hate to see. I mean, couldn’t both teams lose? And, of course, I saw Penn State put another one in the win column with a 42-14 thrashing of Minnesota.

There were a few other games that I caught parts of, but the day was dominated by the operation "get out my wife's Christmas decorations." That leads me to ask my annual question, do you decorate for Christmas before or after Thanksgiving?

Have you seen people putting mustard on Christmas tree cakes?

It's happening. It sounds awful, but I have yet to see a video of someone saying it's as gross as it sounds. I think I'm going to have to let this trend get me.

I'm going to move mustard on Christmas tree cakes to the top of my odd food combinations list. Assuming the trend hasn’t taken off here, and I'm able to find the snack cakes, I'll give this a try and report back.

I don't know who would try this in the first place to see if it was good, but here we are. There's a chance it's an attempt to move product. I'll at least be able to answer whether it tastes good or not.

If you've tried it, let me know what you think.

item.title: Congress' incoming wealthiest member vows to crack down on politicians getting rich in office
item.description: Joe Strada said he plans to crack down on congressional insider trading and politicians enriching themselves, drawing on his rise from bowling alley mechanic.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., poised to become the wealthiest member of Congress, told Fox News Digital that he plans to crack down on politicians who enrich themselves while serving in public office when he takes office in January.

Strada, who went from working as a bowling alley mechanic to owning a nationwide HVAC company, is expected to become Congress' richest member, according to Forbes. The incoming Republican argued that public office should be about serving Americans rather than accumulating personal wealth.

"We need to make sure that we hold politicians accountable," Strada told Fox News Digital. "Nobody, and I mean nobody, should get rich in public office. We're there to serve the American people."

"If you want to get rich, stay in the private sector. I went into business to get rich, not Washington, D.C. I'm going to Washington, D.C., to serve the American people," he continued.

The congressman-elect said combating congressional insider trading and political profiteering would be among his priorities as he prepares to leave the private sector for Capitol Hill.

Strada pointed to his own rise from a blue-collar worker to a successful businessman as proof that the American Dream remains achievable, arguing that excessive government intervention has made it harder for others to follow a similar path.

"I started with nothing. I was a handyman at a bowling alley. If I can do it, other everyday Americans can. Government needs to get out of their way and help them succeed," Strada said. "It's so important to give people opportunity to succeed and achieve their version of the American dream, and now it's time to open that up."

"That's what I plan to do in Washington, D.C., give every American the opportunity they need to succeed, prosper, open a small business and start a career," he added.

"I'm living proof of it," Strada said, referring to his own success.

The incoming Republican also warned that the growing popularity of democratic socialism and proposals for expanding government programs could undermine American entrepreneurship, innovation and small-business growth.

"I think it's important to show people the opportunity. The talking points of ‘free this, free that’ sounds great, but we do not want to suppress the American people. We instead want to show them that their goals and ambitions are achievable," Strada said.

"It was achievable for me. I never went to college, the thought of college was not even in conversation with my parents. Going to college for me was unachievable," he added.

Strada said his early work experience taught him the importance of discipline and perseverance, values he believes should be emphasized to younger generations.

"I knew I had to work, and I worked hard," Strada said, adding that young Americans could benefit from a greater emphasis on work ethic. "I think if we can instill that in young people today, they'd be better off."

The congressman-elect also identified housing affordability as a major obstacle preventing Americans from achieving financial independence, pledging to pursue federal deregulation, lower construction material costs and workforce development initiatives to make homeownership more accessible.

"Housing cost is ridiculous. I have so many examples of ways we can still build a high-quality home for substantially less money, and more Americans could live out their dream of owning a home," Strada said.

As he prepares to take office in January, Strada said he hopes to secure a seat on the House Appropriations Committee, where he believes his business experience would allow him to "best serve the American people."

item.title: Loch Ness Monster sightings jump in 2026 as scientist drills into legendary mystery
item.description: Even though Loch Ness Monster sightings have more than doubled in 2026, a University of St Andrews researcher explains that the spike is "nothing special" in his view.
item.content:encoded:
The Loch Ness Monster is making waves again amid an uptick in reported sightings — but one researcher told Fox News Digital he still isn't convinced the legendary Scottish creature is real.

Reported sightings of Nessie, as the creature is popularly known, have more than doubled in 2026, climbing to 15 from six in 2025, according to the Official Loch Ness Monster Sightings Register.

The register contains eyewitness accounts from visitors and locals around Loch Ness, a freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands, roughly 20 miles southwest of Inverness.

1,000-YEAR-OLD CHURCH MYSTERY CRACKED BY STUDENTS FROM KING CHARLES' ALMA MATER

In March, an American man said he saw "the dark-greenish gray body of what appeared to be Nessie emerge from the water."

The man wrote, according to the register, "Nessie hovered for about 5 seconds, then dipped back into the water. Her body emerged against the chop of the surf, but appeared clearly defined against the waves, leading me to believe it wasn't just the current."

In July, a local sailor said he saw a "large oversized crocodile head above the water" while he was out on his yacht.

"The head quickly disappeared before I could get a photo," the man said. "It took me a few minutes to process what I was seeing. We made it into Fort Augustus safely with no further sightings."

'SIGNIFICANT' EARLY CHRISTIAN CHURCH EMERGES BENEATH FORMER FISH MARKET IN ANCIENT CITY

One visitor from Malta said he saw a creature in August that looked like a "very large eel" moving against the current.

"He estimated that the size was at least 7 meters [about 23 feet] in length," the register stated.

Though the increase in sightings may seem significant, one expert disagrees.

Charles Paxton, a research fellow in statistical ecology at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, told Fox News Digital there was "nothing special" about the jump in reported sightings from 2025 to 2026.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER EERIE ANGLO-SAXON 'SAND BODIES' AT NUCLEAR POWER STATION SITE

"The numbers fluctuate a lot year on year," he said.

Paxton said the modern phenomenon of Loch Ness Monster sightings began in the 1930s, particularly between 1933 and 1934.

The reported sightings quickly became a major draw for tourists, bringing crowds to the area.

"In 1934, the local government slashed its tourist budget, because they felt it wasn't necessary to do any advertising for tourism whatsoever," he said. "And there were traffic jams around the loch."

ARCHAEOLOGISTS FIND ARTIFACTS OLDER THAN STONEHENGE BENEATH BRITAIN'S HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT: 'INCREDIBLY RARE'

That surge of interest fell off over the years, but was revived again in the 1960s when the Loch Ness Investigation Bureau began collecting data on Nessie sightings.

"And then, since the '70s, numbers have generally sort of dwindled, but with fluctuations" from year to year, Paxton said.

Paxton also clarified that the database used to track modern sightings is not an official record, despite its name.

"In a real sense, there isn't an official database," he said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"There are people collecting reports of the Loch Ness Monster from a variety of sources," added Paxton. "But that website has become a central location for people to [share] their reports."

Paxton, who is currently researching how cultural influences may contribute to reported sightings, said statistics can help researchers better understand why people report unusual experiences.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

He and his colleagues have studied patterns in Loch Ness Monster sightings, "mainly for fun, I must admit," he said. 

"And people have these exciting, strange experiences, and the question is, what caused them? And I think we can use statistics to kind of investigate patterns in what's going on."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Though Paxton doesn't believe there is an unknown animal lurking in the loch, he said he doesn't think those who report seeing the monster are lying.

"I don't think that's the case at all," he said.

He cited several possible explanations, including "people seeing animals in the loch, people seeing boat wakes, people seeing wind waves, floating vegetation."

Paxton added, "In my view, the Loch Ness Monster has lots of different sources."

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: What big tech’s weekend from hell means for the future of data centers
item.description: Microsoft Outlook's Thursday shutdown and the FAA's Friday flight grounding highlight why data center advocates say this infrastructure is essential.
item.content:encoded:
The last several days have not been good for big tech. On Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, which handles most of the business email in America, suddenly shut down. Then, on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country, apparently because of technical upgrades that went wrong.

These fiber-optic faceplants happen to come at a moment when much of the country, mostly at the local level, is seeing fierce opposition to data centers, not only because of environmental concerns and energy prices but also because of real concerns that tech is becoming too big a part of our lives.

In Maryland, the story of Taylor Frazier-McCollum, a community activist who helped block a $5 billion data center project planned for the site of an abandoned mall, went viral, with the left praising the power and bravery of the individual and the right mocking her alternative idea for the site: a trampoline park.

INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE'

In fairness, this Maryland activist does not come across as particularly adroit or searing in her insights. On the other hand, like many Americans, she understands implicitly the advantages a trampoline park or a Topgolf location can bring to her community. The benefits of a data center seem murky by comparison.

This kind of attitude toward data centers has many very smart people pulling their hair out in frustration. For them, the economic and technological benefits, including beating China in the AI race, obviously far outweigh the concerns of nonexperts like Frazier-McCollum.

In fact, many proponents of data centers argue that China is funding propaganda to slow our growth in the sector, even as data centers start popping up all over China like umbrella salesmen in a Manhattan rainstorm.

This is true. China, the Eddie Haskell of the planet, is absolutely "giving us the business" by stoking anti-data center fervor. But it is important to remember that data centers aren’t controversial because of Chinese information operations; rather, Chinese information operations exist because data centers are controversial.

FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS

Up until about six months ago, data centers were not a major national news story. In fact, the place one was most likely to hear about them was local talk radio in small towns across rural America, where many people care more about who the county commissioner is than who lives at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.

The concerns you hear from callers on these shows sound downright mundane compared to the fervent calls from experts to win the new space race against China and unleash the power of AI. But for many who live there, water rights and easements mean more than geopolitical fisticuffs.

This is why, in a strange way, this week’s tech mishaps, which inconvenienced millions of Americans at work and at airports, present an opportunity for the tech industry to explain in more practical terms why we need so many data centers.

Implicit in the pro-data center argument has been the idea, often offered with a bit of disdain, that it is absurd to oppose data centers by posting about them on devices that cannot operate without data centers. And OK, point taken, but the snark doesn’t help.

8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS

In fact, Democrats, one could say cynically, capitalized on the anger many Americans felt at being talked down to by the big tech set, using it to great electoral advantage, especially in traditionally right-leaning rural areas. But Democrats, no matter who leads them, cannot maintain their blanket disapproval of data centers for long, as this weekend showed.

It was safe enough to call for data center moratoriums in the races of 2026, but as they seek to govern, Democrats will need data centers. Let’s face it, nobody is going back to typewriters and fax machines, and nobody wants to sit in seat 24B for five hours on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

RED COUNTIES WITH DATA CENTER PROJECTS SWUNG AWAY FROM GOP IN MIDTERMS, ANALYSIS FINDS

At the local level, much of the data center fuss is already working itself out through the sausage-making of politics and the courts. Some communities, like the Amish, will eschew the infrastructure projects completely and lose out on the pot of gold. But most will find a happy compromise once enough concessions are pried from developers.

For now, proponents of data centers would be wise to point to events like the Outlook outage and the flight groundings, without sneering, as the very reason we need so many data centers to power the conveniences we have all grown accustomed to.

With the midterms behind us and our tech infrastructure on thin ice, now is the time for the case to be made that, one way or another, our future lies in data centers.

item.title: LSU mascot Mike the Tiger goes after Texas player after Longhorns stun Tigers in Death Valley
item.description: The clip shows Mike the Tiger charging at Texas wide receiver Chris Stewart after the taunting freshman celebrated in LSU's end zone postgame.
item.content:encoded:
LSU mascot Mike the Tiger had to be held back by his handlers to keep him from getting into a scrap with a Texas player after the Longhorns shocked the Tigers on Saturday night.

If that sentence isn't the perfect summation of SEC football just meaning more, I'm not sure what is.

The wild scene took place in the end zone in front of the LSU student section after several Texas players ran over to dance in front of students following the Horns' 22-21 win. While a few LSU and Texas players were seen jawing back and forth, it was the mascot who seemed the most ready to throw hands.

LSU’S MIKE THE TIGER STALKS REFEREE WHILE DRESSED AS MICHAEL MYERS, APPEARS TO BE STEERED AWAY BY STAFFER

In the mascot's defense, he was simply standing on the field near the end zone when Texas wide receiver Chris Stewart made his way over to taunt him. Stewart, a freshman who didn't catch a pass in the game, was seen jawing with the mascot, to which Mike reacted by going after him.

The funniest part of the clip, without question, is that Mike didn't have just one staff member looking after his well-being, but six poor souls responsible for keeping him out of trouble. To their credit, they did their job.

As for the contest between the Tigers and Longhorns, it undoubtedly lived up to the hype, but served as a season-ender for LSU as the loss handed the Tigers their fourth of the season, killing their dreams of sneaking into the College Football Playoff.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The quarterback play between Texas' Arch Manning and LSU's Sam Leavitt was suboptimal on Saturday, with each signal caller throwing three interceptions, but Manning did just enough to get the job done with his game-winning touchdown pass coming with just two seconds left in regulation.

Texas, which entered the week ranked No. 6 in the latest CFB Playoff rankings, will close out the regular season with matchups against Arkansas and Texas A&M. The Longhorns will be significant favorites in both games, and are suddenly staring at earning a potential first-round bye in the Playoff after dropping back-to-back games in October.

item.title: Richard Sterban of The Oak Ridge Boys dead at 83
item.description: Richard Sterban's iconic bass voice powered The Oak Ridge Boys' "Elvira" to No. 1. His family revealed he battled pancreatic cancer since March.
item.content:encoded:
Richard Sterban, whose unmistakable voice helped make The Oak Ridge Boys’ "Elvira" a country music classic, has died. He was 83.

The singer died Saturday, Nov. 14, in Hendersonville, Tennessee, from complications of bronchitis and pneumonia following a long battle with cancer, according to an announcement from his family and The Oak Ridge Boys.

"We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers. Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time, we find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus," his family said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

Sterban publicly announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis in September 2025, revealing that doctors had diagnosed him that March. Despite his health struggles, the country music veteran expressed hope that his faith and medical care would help him recover and return to performing.

JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71

"With the help of the Good Lord above, I believe I will be able to get through this," he said at the time. He also thanked fans for their prayers and said he hoped to return to the road within several months.

NEW PANCREATIC CANCER PILL COULD RESHAPE TREATMENT AS EARLY TRIAL RESULTS STUN RESEARCHERS

After stepping away from touring in May 2025, Sterban returned to the Grand Ole Opry on Jan. 30 and 31, 2026, joining his bandmates for performances of "Elvira" that brought audiences to their feet, according to the announcement.

"Having Richard on stage with us again was one of God’s greatest blessings," fellow Oak Ridge Boys singer Duane Allen said.

GEORGE STRAIT PULLS OFF INCREDIBLE CAREER ACCOMPLISHMENT WITH STUNNING CONCERT

Born April 24, 1943, in Camden, New Jersey, Sterban began singing in Sunday school at age 6. His voice transitioned from soprano to bass by eighth grade, setting him on a path that would eventually take him from gospel quartets to some of music’s biggest stages.

Before joining The Oak Ridge Boys, Sterban performed behind Elvis Presley as a member of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet. He toured and recorded with Presley and appeared in the 1972 concert film, "Elvis on Tour."

Later that year, he left the job to become The Oak Ridge Boys’ bass singer.

"I wanted to be in the best vocal group in the world," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Alongside lead singer Allen, baritone William Lee Golden and tenor Joe Bonsall, Sterban helped transform the Southern gospel quartet into a country and pop crossover act. Their hits included "Y’all Come Back Saloon," "Bobbie Sue," and "American Made."

But it was Sterban’s booming bass refrain on the group’s 1981 recording of "Elvira" that became his musical calling card. The song reached No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on the pop chart and earned a Grammy Award.

OUTLAW COUNTRY SINGER DAVID ALLAN COE DEAD AT 86

"It’s the song everyone hopes to hear at our concerts," Sterban said on its 40th anniversary, according to the announcement.

The group became Grand Ole Opry members in 2011 and entered the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015.

DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80

Their decades together also forged deep personal bonds.

In January 2021, Allen reflected on his relationship with Sterban, Golden and Bonsall.

"I think the four of us have grown closer than we’ve ever been in our whole career," Allen told Fox News Digital at the time.

RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

item.title: Virginia parents charged after house party draws hundreds of teens, fireworks and alleged underage drinking
item.description: Fairfax County police charged Lisa and Aubrey Vaughan after their 13-year-old sons' small backyard party spiraled into a massive gathering with fireworks and crowds.
item.content:encoded:
A Virginia couple who say they wanted to give their 13-year-old sons a safe place to hang out with a handful of classmates ended up facing criminal charges after their backyard gathering exploded into a massive party with hundreds of teenagers, fireworks and police descending on their neighborhood.

Lisa Vaughan, 45, and Aubrey Vaughan, 55, were charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance after Fairfax County police responded to their McLean home on Nov. 6. The couple maintains their innocence, with their attorney saying an invitation intended for just 10 to 20 classmates spread to older students.

"There will be no more," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5 DC, referring to the party for their sons. "We're done."

COLLEGE HOMECOMING PARTY TURNS TO CHAOS AS DECK COLLAPSES, LEAVING AT LEAST 28 PEOPLE INJURED

Police responded to multiple 911 calls around 9:03 p.m. reporting an out-of-control party. Callers estimated between 100 and 300 people had gathered at the home, where responding officers encountered a large crowd and fireworks being discharged, according to police.

Aubrey Vaughan apologized to neighbors, saying he was "embarrassed" by how quickly the gathering spiraled out of control. He and his wife even had their 13-year-old sons go door-to-door to apologize after police dispersed the crowd, according to FOX 5.

The couple had planned a small eighth-grade gathering, but the invitation circulated on Snapchat and eventually reached students at a local high school, attracting uninvited teenagers, according to the family's attorney.

Aubrey Vaughan said he had "zero idea" high schoolers would show up and that he and his wife struggled to keep them out of their backyard and home.

Police described the gathering as an "underage drinking party," but Vaughan disputed suggestions that alcohol was permitted. He told FOX 5 that the invitation explicitly prohibited alcohol and bags, and that he and his wife were home supervising the entire time.

Aubrey Vaughan estimated the incident lasted about 45 minutes, saying he realized things were getting out of hand roughly 10 to 15 minutes before officers arrived.

"They wanted to maintain a safe place, free from alcohol, for kids to have a good time, but they had no control about all the kids that arrived and caused chaos in their neighborhood," the couple's attorney, Alaric Piette, told FOX 5.

Piette said the parents welcomed officers and offered to let them inspect the party area, but police declined. Both parents later turned themselves in and were released on $1,000 unsecured bonds each.

FAMILIES CONFRONT CALIFORNIA 'PARTY MOM' IN COURT, CALLING HER A 'MONSTER' WHO GROOMED THEIR CHILDREN

Fairfax County Police Chief Kevin Davis acknowledged the challenges parents face when deciding whether to host gatherings at home rather than let teenagers socialize elsewhere without supervision.

"I think it's universally a bad idea to host anything at a home," Davis said, warning that large gatherings involving alcohol, drugs or reckless behavior can quickly become dangerous.

The police chief emphasized that "parents have to be parents" and "adults have to be adults," warning that good intentions can have unintended consequences.

Aubrey Vaughan, meanwhile, said he was grateful police helped disperse the crowd and harbors no resentment toward the responding officers.

"The lesson is just make sure you're watching Snapchat," Aubrey Vaughan told FOX 5.

Police have not announced charges against any teenagers who attended the gathering.

item.title: Putin's war machine tied to troubling recruitment of young women as new deals emerge
item.description: Two African governments signed deals with Russia's Alabuga drone factory zone as a Ukrainian probe alleges deceptive recruitment of young African women.
item.content:encoded:
Two African governments have signed new agreements with a Russian industrial complex linked to the production of attack drones used against Ukraine, even as a Ukrainian investigation alleges Moscow is expanding a recruitment network that draws young African women into its military-industrial workforce.

The agreements, signed in late October by Ghana and the Democratic Republic of the Congo with Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, come months after Britain sanctioned individuals and entities associated with the Alabuga Start program over deceptive recruitment practices. The new partnerships raise questions about whether Russia's efforts to attract foreign workers could help sustain drone production as its war against Ukraine continues.

The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre says it has obtained internal documents identifying approximately 50 African women employed at Alabuga, alongside 10 Russian recruiters and two African intermediaries allegedly involved in attracting foreign workers.

OUR ADVERSARIES ARE EVEN USING THE US BANKING SYSTEM. HERE’S HOW THEY GET AWAY WITH IT

"What we were able to do is basically to obtain internal documentation," Solomiya Khoma, the organization's head of international cooperation, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Khoma said the investigation went beyond previous reporting by attempting to establish how recruitment operates across borders, connecting Russian cultural organizations, local intermediaries and Alabuga's human resources department. "Our case is specifically related to African countries," she said.

According to the report, the alleged network operates on three levels: Russian cultural and educational organizations cultivating relationships with young people in Africa, local recruiters promoting opportunities abroad, and Alabuga personnel arranging employment and logistics.

The investigation identifies two women from Tunisia and Uganda as alleged recruitment coordinators and describes connections with Russian HR personnel and foreign employees. Their specific recruitment activities have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital.

Khoma said the findings relied partly on a confidential source who remains employed within the Alabuga industrial complex.

"This person is still continuing to work in the Alabuga economical zone and these factories," she said, explaining why the organization could not disclose the source's identity.

She said investigators obtained information about the workers and their identities, including internal employee passes.

The researchers also examined the involvement of Russian cultural organizations, including councils of Russian compatriots and the Russkiy Mir Foundation, in promoting educational and employment opportunities in African countries.

The report points to a September 2024 cooperation memorandum between the Russian compatriots' council in Tunisia and Alabuga, alongside Russian cultural activities in Uganda. However, the investigation does not establish that Russian diplomats or cultural organizations knowingly directed recruits into military drone production.

The findings build on an Associated Press investigation published in October 2024, which documented how African women recruited with promises of education and civilian employment were assigned to manufacture Iranian-designed attack drones. Some described long hours, lower-than-promised wages, surveillance and exposure to hazardous chemicals.

Khoma described a recruitment process in which women arrive in Russia expecting to combine education with paid employment, only to fail entrance examinations or Russian-language requirements.

"These people are promised a dual education opportunity," she said.

After failing examinations, she alleged, workers may find themselves with limited options and unable to afford transportation home, leaving them performing factory work instead of pursuing their expected studies.

The recruitment program has also attracted international scrutiny. On May 5, 2026, the British government sanctioned seven individuals and entities associated with Alabuga Start recruitment, accusing the operation of using deceptive practices to obtain foreign labor for facilities producing military drones.

Yet cooperation with African governments appears to be continuing.

US COMPANIES WIN BILLIONS IN AFRICAN DATA CENTER DEALS IN DIRECT COMPETITION WITH CHINA

Ghanaian broadcaster Citi News reported October 29 that Labor Minister Emmanuel Agyekum signed an agreement with Alabuga to facilitate industrial employment opportunities for Ghanaian citizens. The ministry said it would coordinate recruitment, verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation.

Meanwhile, CongoRassure reported October 30 that the Democratic Republic of the Congo signed a five-year memorandum focused on vocational training and strengthening employment institutions.

Neither agreement, as publicly described, establishes that either government intended to supply workers for military production.

Khoma called for sanctions targeting the recruitment networks themselves, including intermediaries, financial channels and organizations facilitating foreign labor recruitment.

She argued that Russia's efforts to attract workers from abroad reflect growing labor shortages across its wartime economy and represent another potential point of international pressure.

"Without this effort abroad, without this help abroad, it would be difficult for Russia to sustain a war longer," she said.

Fox News Digital has reached out for comment to Alabuga, the Russian Foreign Ministry, and government representatives in Ghana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda and Tunisia.

item.title: Johnny Depp fled Hollywood spotlight for quiet Bahamas life where 'nobody’s pointing a camera at me'
item.description: Johnny Depp opens up about how his 1940s Bahamas wood house with a yurt and painting studio became his sanctuary away from cameras and fame.
item.content:encoded:
Johnny Depp turns to the Bahamas to experience a private life.

During an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Depp opened up about craving privacy and not being able to have it in the United States.

"Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody’s pointing a camera at me or staring. I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me," Depp told the outlet.

‘GREASE’ STAR STOCKARD CHANNING SAYS SHE’S ‘HAPPY BEING A RECLUSE’ AFTER LEAVING AMERICA

Depp famously purchased his own island in the Bahamas in 2004. In 2009, he told Vanity Fair that "escapism is survival to me," and that, after playing a difficult role, "my head was done in. I needed to escape. So being able to get on the boat and move allowed my head freedom again."

He continued, "Somehow, the mathematics led me here to my island. I don’t think I’d ever seen any place so pure and beautiful. You can feel your pulse rate drop about 20 beats. It’s instant freedom. And that rare beast—simplicity—can be had. And a little morsel of anonymity."

The actor added, "Whenever I was getting frustrated about being ‘novelty boy’ and making movies, I told myself, Calm down. I can come down here and disappear."

Depp told SCMP Style in 2023, "Where I feel the most myself in this world, and where I go to feel absolutely normal, I suppose, is my place in the Bahamas, because it’s an island and nobody’s looking at me. You’ve got to have some sanctuary, a safe place where you can escape the scrutiny and the interest of others, a place where you can just sit on a beach, read, paint, meditate or whatever, that’s freedom to me. That’s the only real freedom."

Making music is also something Depp likes to do on his island. Telling WSJ about how he passes his time there, he said, "I like to grab about four or five books and flop on the couch and read. Or I play guitar in my music studio." 

In the 80s, Depp was in a band – music was what originally brought him to Los Angeles in 1983, not acting.

"Soon after, I met actor Nicolas Cage at a friend’s house. Nic came to see my band several times, and we became friends," Depp said. "Six months later, he suggested I try acting. I was up for anything that would help pay the bills."

Depp went on to become a household name thanks to movies like "Edward Scissorhands" and "What's Eating Gilbert Grape."

He is now starring in his first major Hollywood film in eight years. Depp stars as the title role in "Ebenezer," which debuted on Friday.

"There was a great veil lifted when my first child was born. And suddenly, I understood exactly what everything had been for," Depp said. "There were years of that, that I thought, ‘What am I doing? Why am I doing these movies?’ This is what it's all about."

item.title: Luxury real estate expert reveals benefits of Kirk Cousins selling his home privately after trade to Vikings
item.description: Kirk Cousins sold his Minnesota home off-market through a neighbor before joining the Atlanta Falcons, avoiding the public listing process entirely.
item.content:encoded:
While Kirk Cousins is back in Minnesota with the Vikings, not everything will be quite the same.

Cousins revealed that when he signed with the Atlanta Falcons in 2024, he sold his house through a neighbor without ever putting it on the open market. The 38-year-old said his neighbor told him he had someone who could buy his house immediately, so Cousins sold it without ever listing it.

Margit Brandt, a luxury real estate agent, said that Cousins may have gotten a little lucky finding an off the market buyer for his house so quickly, but there are many advantages to selling a home off-market.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Another component to the off-market is also privacy and discretion and not having your name out there because when you publicly list something, press picks it up. There's photos on Zillow and online of like what your living room and your kitchen and your closet, like all these personal spaces," Brandt told OutKick in a recent interview.

"So for someone like Kirk Cousins to have someone come in off market and not have to like open his dress, so to speak, right, in terms of his home on the market, his name being out there. I think that's appealing."

Brandt is based in Palm Beach, Florida, and said her team has sold $1 billion worth of homes this year, with about a third of those sales completed off-market. When looking to sell a home, Brandt said she taps into her relationships if a client initially requests an off-market sale.

"We have like a private portfolio for off-market properties. And you have good broker relationships and you have to know the market and we have 30% of the Palm Beach market right now. So we know exactly who's looking at what price point, who's real, who's not. It gives you a good bird's eye view of like what's happening here," Brandt said.

"So, you can certainly try something off-market for all those reasons we just discussed, privacy, discretion, safety, even, right? People don't want people to know where they live. It's a safety thing."

Cousins said at the end of his re-introductory press conference with the Minnesota Vikings that his wife, Julie, and their sons are staying in a hotel while she looks for a new home. The Pro Bowl quarterback hopes to find their next home sooner rather than later.

"Trust me, because we sell a lot of houses, it's harder than it looks. It's sometimes it takes a little bit to get to the right person for every house, but there is a person for every house. We've learned that there is," Brandt said.

item.title: Simple salt substitute could prevent three million deaths a year worldwide, study estimates
item.description: A Nature Health study finds potassium salt substitutes could prevent nearly 3 million deaths yearly, but hyperkalemia poses risks for some patients.
item.content:encoded:
Replacing regular table salt with a potassium-enriched alternative could prevent nearly three million deaths and more than 10 million cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide every year, according to a major study published in Nature Health.

Researchers at the Australia-based George Institute for Global Health analyzed dietary patterns and disease risks among 4.6 billion adults across 193 countries to estimate the potential benefits of the switch.

The study relied on mathematical simulations rather than a clinical trial, using estimates that can vary in accuracy, the researchers acknowledged.

HIGH SALT INTAKE LINKED TO FASTER MEMORY DECLINE IN ONE GROUP, STUDY FINDS

High blood pressure affects roughly 1.4 billion adults worldwide and is a leading cause of strokes, heart attacks and chronic kidney damage, according to the World Health Organization.

Consuming too much salt can contribute to high blood pressure, as its sodium content causes the body to retain water, increasing blood volume and putting added pressure on artery walls.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some sodium with potassium while looking, tasting and cooking like regular salt. The swap reduces sodium intake while boosting potassium, which helps relax blood vessels and promotes the removal of excess sodium from the body, according to the researchers.

If households replaced only the salt used in home cooking and at the dining table, the model projected 1.85 million fewer deaths and 6.19 million fewer new cases of heart and kidney disease annually.

ANCIENT CHINESE MOVEMENT SHOWS PROMISE FOR REDUCING BLOOD PRESSURE AT HOME, STUDY SAYS

In another scenario, replacing salt only in restaurant meals and processed foods was projected to prevent about 1.56 million deaths and 5.46 million new disease cases annually.

In a more targeted scenario, researchers projected that switching 80% of adults with diagnosed high blood pressure to potassium-enriched household salt could prevent about 590,000 deaths worldwide each year.

The projected benefits varied by region, depending on population size and sources of dietary sodium. The largest potential benefit was seen in China, with an estimated 1.08 million deaths averted each year under full replacement. 

India followed with nearly 400,000 preventable deaths, while the U.S. could potentially avoid roughly 105,000 deaths and 492,000 new disease cases annually.

POPULAR FOOD COULD BOOST HEART HEALTH, BUT THE AMOUNT YOU NEED TO EAT MAY SURPRISE YOU

In many Asian and African countries, most dietary salt comes from home cooking, suggesting that greater awareness and access to potassium-enriched alternatives could encourage healthier habits, according to the researchers.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Broader adoption by food manufacturers and restaurants would be needed to maximize the health benefits in Western countries, where more than 70% of dietary sodium comes from processed and restaurant foods, the study suggested.

"This study shows that small changes have an enormous impact on two prominent diseases globally: cardiovascular disease and kidney disease," Dr. Nathan Goodyear of the Williams Cancer Institute in California told Fox News Digital.

Goodyear, who was not involved in the study, said the bigger take-home message is that health is "not something that we’re just born with."

"It’s something that we cultivate. It’s the environment we cultivate," he said. "And this environment influences the potential for disease harvest long before disease is diagnosed."

While the study's models suggested that the heart health benefits outweighed the risks for the overall population, experts cautioned that the substitute may not be safe for everyone.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Potassium-enriched salt substitutes can also pose risks, including hyperkalemia, a condition in which excess potassium builds up in the blood and can trigger dangerous irregular heart rhythms, according to the National Kidney Foundation.

The body normally removes excess potassium through urine, but people with advanced kidney disease or those taking certain blood pressure medications may have difficulty eliminating it.

The World Health Organization advises against potassium-enriched salt substitutes for people with kidney problems that impair potassium removal, unless recommended by a healthcare professional.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We’re constantly in medicine looking for the magic bullet in causation, magic bullet in disease treatment, [but] that does not exist," said Goodyear.

Chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes and cancer often develop over time due to multiple contributing factors, the doctor noted.

Widespread adoption could also face challenges, as potassium-enriched salt costs about twice as much as regular salt on average and would require cooperation from food manufacturers and suppliers, according to the researchers.

item.title: Trump's top officials retreat behind military gates as ex-FBI deputy points to what's fueling threats
item.description: Scott Bessent joins Todd Blanche, Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth at Washington D.C. military bases amid Iranian assassination threats.
item.content:encoded:
Military bases around Washington, D.C., have become an increasingly common refuge for some of President Donald Trump's most powerful officials, as threats linked to Iran and a surge in threats against public officials raise security concerns across the administration.

"So you have this combination of a permission structure on the left for violence, combine it with the ability to track it and create a long paper trail, and the numbers explode, and these threat matrices go crazy," former Secret Service agent and former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest senior administration official to relocate to a military installation, joining a growing number of top Trump officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats that extend well beyond the White House.

IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the Secretary’s Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the Secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety. The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials," a source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital.

Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, but did not elaborate.

The Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials.

Attorney General Todd Blanche also relocated to a military base from his home around March, a different source familiar with the arrangements told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

The Justice Department charged a member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2022 in an alleged murder-for-hire plot targeting former Trump national security adviser John Bolton, while prosecutors disclosed in 2024 that another Iranian operative had allegedly been tasked with developing a plan to assassinate Trump.

Bongino said federal protection decisions are generally driven by threat assessments that account for threatening communications, social media activity and intelligence gathered by security personnel. Agencies responsible for protecting senior officials use those assessments to determine what level of protection is necessary.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran said last month that threats against the agency's full-time protectees had increased more than 40% from the previous year, with roughly 10,000 threat cases recorded in 2026 at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Secret Service for comment.

"Pretty much, sadly, anyone at the cabinet, or even sub-cabinet level, with any kind of public persona in the Trump administration, needed a detail," Bongino said.

US EVACUATES 13 MILITARY AIRCRAFT FROM SECOND UK BASE AS NEW IRAN THREAT RAISES ALARM

The assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and multiple attempts on President Donald Trump's life have heightened concerns about political violence, as security officials confront a growing volume of threats against public officials.

Bongino pointed to his own experience as FBI deputy director, saying his security needs were comparable to those of some of the government's highest-ranking law enforcement officials.

"Mine was on par with the attorney general and the FBI director that we had to expand it," Bongino said of his threat assessment and security detail. "It was an independent analysis."

Bongino said social media has made threats against public officials easier to track, but the sheer volume of online activity has also created more work for investigators trying to determine which threats are credible.

SECRET SERVICE CHIEF SAYS THREATS AGAINST PROTECTEES UP 40%, CITES INTERNET AND MENTAL HEALTH

Bongino said the disruption to Bessent's personal life underscores the seriousness of the security concerns surrounding his move.

"For him to have to uproot his life. And move on to a military facility where the housing's not terrible in those places, but it's certainly not what he's used to," Bongino said. "This stuff, it's not a convenience issue, I can promise you that. This is definitely serious stuff."

Lawmakers have also raised concerns about security and federal spending. Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., secured House Armed Services Committee approval in June for a proposal seeking a Pentagon report on political appointees living in military housing, including the threats justifying their moves, legal authority for the arrangements and rental costs.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., also questioned whether the reported transfer of $415 million in Secret Service funding to White House construction projects could affect the agency's protective operations, citing federal watchdog concerns about staffing and resource shortages.

Barry Donadio, a former Secret Service agent who served during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, similarly told Fox News Digital that the decision to relocate Bessent to a military installation suggests an extraordinary level of concern among those responsible for his protection.

"My first inkling is that the [threat] is so high that they cannot protect him with certainty, unless he is on a military base which speaks volumes for the situation at hand," Donadio said.

TRUMP ADMIN APPROVES $351 MILLION FOR WHITE HOUSE SECURITY MEASURES AMID QUESTIONS OVER BALLROOM FUNDING

Donadio said the move could indicate that officials believe Bessent would be safer on a military base than at a private residence.

"They may have foiled an attack already that is not being publicized, and as an extra measure, have moved him to a military base for protective custody," Donadio said, clarifying that he did not mean Bessent was in custody, but rather under heightened government protection.

Bessent is not the only senior Trump administration official whose security concerns have prompted a move to military housing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing.

TRUMP ADMIN APPROVES $351 MILLION FOR WHITE HOUSE SECURITY MEASURES AMID QUESTIONS OVER BALLROOM FUNDING

The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence, while Bessent's move comes amid reported threats linked to Iran.

Bongino said threats against high-profile officials can also extend beyond their time in government, describing an incident in which an individual allegedly appeared at a California television studio with a manifesto threatening him and other officials.

"I mean, this stuff is real, it happens every day," Bongino said. "And when you're living through it and you're not accustomed to it, you know, and it follows you after office too."

He said officials including Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Hegseth understood that public service in the administration could make them targets even after leaving office.

Fort McNair, a historic Army installation along the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., has emerged as one of the military properties housing senior Trump administration officials. The installation, which dates to the late 1700s, is home to the National Defense University and traditionally provides residential quarters for senior military leaders.

Fort McNair's residential quarters are divided into two housing groups, according to a 2020 National Capital Planning Commission report, while a 2024 Army filing identifies 27 historic homes built before 1919 at the installation.

The Army's housing website lists 88 historic dwelling units across Fort McNair and nearby Fort Myer combined, without specifying how many are at each base.

The growing use of military housing by senior civilian officials also raises questions about who approves the arrangements, whether officials pay for their accommodations and what impact, if any, the moves have on housing traditionally reserved for military personnel.

item.title: CHUCK DEVORE: Texas turns blue, but here’s where the next 4 big battles are coming
item.description: Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa's new agenda could reshape Texas on taxes, spending, regulation, DEI policy, border security and Operation Lone Star.
item.content:encoded:
After November’s election verdict, Texas isn’t doomed to become California overnight — but not for a lack of trying.

As in much of America (Florida excepted), Texas saw major midterm losses for a Republican Party that has dominated the Lone Star State for the past quarter century. Inauguration Day in 2027, all statewide executive offices were held by Republicans — now the opposite will be the case.

Democrats took the state House of Representatives, but Republicans still hold the state Senate. Republicans also retain a one-vote margin on the state Supreme Court, and the state’s powerful Railroad Commission (the agency that regulates the oil and gas industry, gas utilities, pipeline safety and surface coal and uranium mining) will have a 2-to-1 Republican majority.

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Democrat Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa will bring Texans an entirely new set of priorities and a vastly different style of governance. She began her career as a labor attorney, including working for a powerful government union. In 2005, she was on the legal team that pursued lawfare against then-Republican House Majority Leader Tom DeLay on money-laundering charges.

DeLay was driven from office, convicted in 2010 and fully acquitted in 2014 — the process is the punishment. Before her election to the Texas House in 2016, Hinojosa served on the board of trustees for the Austin Independent School District, a district that has struggled with declining enrollment and the threat of state takeover after campuses received five consecutive failing accountability ratings.

How might Texas under Hinojosa’s leadership fare? Here are four things to watch.

TEXAS GOVERNOR-ELECT'S PLAN TO FREEZE ELECTRICITY PRICES RAISES QUESTIONS OVER LEGAL AUTHORITY

For decades, Texas has benefited from lower taxes and a smaller, less intrusive government than peer-state rivals such as California, Illinois and New York. The population has soared as millions of Americans — and foreign nationals — sought opportunity. That is unlikely to change overnight. What is likely is incremental slippage as other states, notably Florida and Tennessee, work to attract talent and investment.

11TH-HOUR POWER PLAY TARGETS INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR AFTER HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT

Texas last passed major tort reform in 2003 and has seen its national lawsuit-climate ranking slip since then. Hinojosa’s ascent likely means a gradual strengthening of the state’s trial bar at the expense of economic growth.

Ironically, it will likely also increase the cost of living — with affordability an explicit promise of the incoming Democratic leadership. Further, Texas’s innovative Business Court and the Fifteenth Court of Appeals, both created in 2023, saw all three Republican members of the Fifteenth Court lose to Democrats. This flip may tilt the landscape against larger employers when interpreting the scope and power of state regulatory actions.

ONE INDUSTRY FACES MULTI-TRILLION-DOLLAR RECKONING AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION RESHUFFLE

Hinojosa has already moved against billionaire Elon Musk’s plans to expand SpaceX’s Starbase site in Cameron County. Given the governor-elect was part of the lawfare posse that destroyed DeLay, will Hinojosa and her lieutenants resist the urge to go after Musk personally at the risk of harming job creation and innovation in Texas?

Here is where Hinojosa’s victory may have a significant long-term effect. She is positioned to reverse strictures that banned the use of so-called diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) in hiring and curriculum, especially in the university system. Her appointments to higher-education governing boards could reverse many of the commonsense gains made under outgoing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, including the 2023 ban on DEI offices and related practices.

HOUSTON MAYOR BOLTS EARLY FROM ICE COOPERATION AFTER BLUE WAVE CRASHES IN TEXAS

Here Hinojosa’s campaign promises could have an immediate and dramatic effect. Texas has worked alongside the federal government under Republican President Donald Trump, and in spite of the federal government under former Democrat President Joe Biden, to secure its roughly 1,254-mile border with Mexico.

The state’s effort — with National Guard soldiers and Department of Public Safety troopers — aims to protect Texans’ health and welfare by interdicting transnational human smuggling and drug-cartel operations, which include the use of increasingly sophisticated and deadly drones.

BORDER DEM POISED TO WIELD ICE PURSE STRINGS REJECTS SOCIALIST ‘DEFUND’ PUSH

The federal government has some 12,000 to 19,000 Border Patrol, Customs, DEA and active-duty military personnel deployed along the border in Texas at any given time. The state of Texas, through Operation Lone Star, has augmented that with up to 5,500 Guard soldiers and 1,600 DPS troopers for a total of up to 7,000 personnel — meaning Texas provides about one out of every two people guarding the long Rio Grande frontier.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Ending Texas’s border effort removes thousands of state law-enforcement and surveillance personnel from the border. The result could be more deadly fentanyl, more human trafficking, and more dangerous illegal aliens successfully crossing into Texas and causing death and injury. All of this could be avoidable, and it is unlikely that the voters who gave Hinojosa her margin of victory were fully aware of this portion of her platform.

Texas’s long-run advantages in taxes, regulation and energy will not vanish on inauguration day. But the direction of travel for the next four years is now clear, and the four areas above will show how quickly — and how far — the state embraces California-style dysfunction.
